nodes.title: What persuasion means
nodes.body:

One important limit: Strong emotion during persuasion is not automatically coercion.

nodes.scenario: Asha is considering a job offer in another city. Her partner Ben wants her to stay, and they are talking after dinner.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'd like to take the interview. It doesn't mean I've decided to move.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I'll miss you if you go. I think that matters too.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It does. We can talk about how we'd manage the distance.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: After everything I've done for you, I don't think you should even be considering it.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Not every attempt to persuade someone or every refusal to fund a partner's choices is coercion. Look for conditions, power and a recurring pattern.
checks.counterexample: Not every attempt to persuade someone or every refusal to fund a partner's choices is coercion. Look for conditions, power and a recurring pattern.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Not every attempt to persuade someone or every refusal to fund a partner's choices is coercion. Look for conditions, power and a recurring pattern.
nodes.sources: Stark (2007), Coercive Control; behaviour analysis of contingencies; UK Domestic Abuse Act 2021 guidance.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.

lessons.title: When a favour becomes a test
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of persuasion versus manipulation.

nodes.title: What might be happening?
nodes.body:
Persuasion gives somebody reasons to reconsider. Manipulative pressure can make an unrelated personal cost depend on compliance. Here, the proposed cost is being regarded as a disloyal friend. Whether this was deliberate matters less to Nina's immediate decision than the pressure the statement creates.

Reminding someone of a past favour is not automatically manipulation. Repetition, freedom to decline and how the disagreement is handled change the judgement.
nodes.sources: Cialdini, Influence; Linehan, DBT interpersonal effectiveness.

glossary.definition: Trying to change a person's view by giving reasons they can consider and reject.
glossary.example: A partner explains why a move would be difficult and asks to discuss alternatives.
glossary.limit: Strong emotion during persuasion is not automatically coercion.

glossary.definition: Steering a decision through misleading information or pressure that conceals or distorts the choice available.
glossary.example: Someone claims a favour is proof of loyalty while withholding facts that would change the decision.
glossary.limit: We need evidence of how the influence works, rather than guessing someone's hidden intention.

glossary.definition: Using a threat or a serious cost to reduce another person's freedom to choose.
glossary.example: A person threatens to withdraw essential support unless their partner turns down an interview.
glossary.limit: A genuine independent budget limit needs to be distinguished from a punishment tied to compliance.

glossary.definition: A pattern in which someone undermines another person's confidence in their memory or judgement of reality.
glossary.example: A person repeatedly denies documented events and uses the other's confusion as proof they cannot be trusted.
glossary.limit: A disagreement about an event, or an honest memory error, is not enough on its own.
